paras: The threatened lynching of Michael Reinhart took place at Winamac, Indiana, on the evening of September 13, 1888, after Reinhart, a barber, shot and killed the contractor Joseph W. Robinson in a saloon. A crowd threatened to lynch him, and the sheriff guarded the jail with a large force until the danger passed. Reinhart was convicted of murder two months later and sentenced to life imprisonment.

Robinson, about thirty-five, contracted to drill gas and oil wells and had come to Winamac from Francesville with others to attend court. He and Reinhart had had "some previous trouble," though the Indianapolis Journal's correspondent wrote that no one seemed to know the particulars.

At dusk, as the Francesville party prepared to leave, Robinson stepped into Deutsch's saloon and offered to make friends when Reinhart came in. According to both Winamac specials, Reinhart answered "All right," then drew a revolver and shot Robinson at close range, killing him instantly. Reinhart fled, failed to board a train for Logansport, and was found about half an hour later hiding under a stairway in his barber shop, where he surrendered without a struggle.

The Indiana State Sentinel's correspondent wrote that Reinhart gave himself up "begging protection of the authorities from the infuriated crowd." A wire report went further, saying he "barely escaped being lynched before the sheriff could get him to the jail." The sheriff then summoned a strong guard; the wire put it at one hundred men and reported parties prowling around the jail at 2 o'clock in the morning. The Sentinel described the guard as the sheriff's posse, posted for fear of an attack by friends of the dead man, who according to the wire swore to avenge his death.

No attack on the jail was reported. An Illinois weekly's summary of news for the week ended November 20, 1888, reported that Reinhart had been convicted on Saturday of Robinson's murder and sentenced to life imprisonment.

The first reports were specials from Winamac dated September 13 in the Indianapolis Journal and the Indiana State Sentinel. Both called Robinson "a highly respected citizen" and described Reinhart as "a gambler and a drunkard" and "a local tough," while predicting that "better counsel" would prevail over the lynching talk.

A shorter wire version, which made Robinson "a prominent and wealthy oil contractor of Lima, O.," ran in New Haven on September 15 under the headline "In Cold Blood" and in Maysville, Kentucky, the same day. It was reprinted as a brief in the Yorkville Enquirer in South Carolina on September 19 and the Cambria Freeman in Pennsylvania on September 21, framed around the murder and the guard against lynching rather than the crowd. No paper gave the race of anyone involved.

The Indiana specials, filed the night of the shooting, gave Robinson's home as Francesville, Indiana, while the wire placed it at Lima, Ohio. The specials spoke only of talk and threats of lynching, whereas the wire said Reinhart narrowly escaped a lynching on the way to jail, and the Yorkville Enquirer dated the shooting to Friday night rather than Thursday.

bases: A crowd threatened to lynch Reinhart after the shooting and the wire says he barely escaped being lynched on the way to jail, where an armed guard was posted; no one was killed by the crowd (A1, A2, A4).
Reinhart was threatened by a crowd over the killing of Robinson, but he was jailed, guarded and later tried and sentenced, so no one was killed by the crowd (A2, A4, A7).
